&90 I love dynamics. I love having something surprising in the middle of an otherwise, sort-of, predictable environment.

&92 I just gave James the mister drones and the pop-up mister, and I said you can use this wherever you want as many times you want. Wherever you want amongst the little plants.

&93 And I really love the order he gave it. It really gives the scene a bit of character, I think. So that's an animation I did just as a throwaway thing, I think it became the highlight of the scene for me.
&100 I actually really struggled getting this scene to a point where I was happy with it. For some reason the elements didn't come together very well for me.
&101 But adding the foreground plants somehow really made the scene for me.

&102 I'm not sure what it is about them that I like so much, but I think they break up what is otherwise a very 3D looking scene. It looks very artificial to me. Adding those in saved it for me personally.
&103 I'm not sure if anybody else thinks that, but it's nice for me to be able to look at it and go "Yeah that's done it. That's done the job."

&110 I actually though it was a little bit much to have two seperate scenes for a single location split up by a parallax foreground layer, but when I saw the final thing working I thought that James is a clever fellow.

&111 It does mean that you have to do to seperate scenes for the location, but I really like how the effect worked out. And blocking off the transition with that foreground layer was a very clever idea. So good thinking, James.
&112 I also only only did one spinning fan animation, and James just reused it a lot. So I can't complain that it was too much work. Because I cheated.
&120 My friend Ivan Ulyanov - great guy, great artist - he did the portraits that you are seeing in this game. Including this one you're seeing right now of my face.
&121 He recommended to me that I read a comic series called Transmetropolitan as a cyberpunk influence. And I adored Transmetropolitan. It was a great read.

&122 I really, really love Spider Jerusalem as a character. So in this little scene, as a little tribute to both Ivan and the comic series, I put in the three eyed smiley face and also a little spider above it.

&130 It's kind of funny. This location - just like the driving scene - is really just a location hub. There's not much to do. There's one guy to get past. And somehow it became one of the most elaborate things to construct in the game.
&131 I think I might have gotten a little bit carried away from what James's original vision was, but I really love the way it turned out.
&140 If you look over to the right, you'll see some letters stencilled on the machinery. Which those of you who have played another Wadjet Eye Game (Primordia) might recognize.
&141 I really love Vic's artwork in that game. Vic's a really nice guy and I really like talking to him and I wanted to make a reference to that game in here somewhere. So that's where I did it.
&150 I love graffiti in game locations. I think it adds a really human touch to what can otherwise look like what some man or lady sitting at a desk has just drawn. Which is what it is.
&151 A friend of mine, Sebastian, once told me that graffiti is there for a reason. People just want to express themselves for a reason, or they want to make their presense known.
&160 When James told me he wanted to have this guy have a virus put him in a prison inside his own mind, I wasn't really sure what to do.
&161 But I like Doom. And I like how Doom uses nice panoramic photos as a backdrop for Hell. So I thought, why don't I get a nice photo of a nice sky and turn it into this horrible red color.
&162 So you have Doom to thank for the way this turned out.
&170 When you think of cyberpunk you always think of the dark, neon-soaked streets of a grimy city. And it wasn't until this point in the game that we actually ended up doing that sort of scene.

&180 James had this idea that he wanted cyberspace should look very different from the real world. I wanted all the characters to have a kind of different style. Much like peoples' avatars on online forums, etc.

&181 And I did different styles for as many of the different characters as I could, and also tried to make none of them look like real world characters. I wanted everybody to be their own sort of person.
&182 So that explains the kind of incongruous styles here. I'm not sure it really carries over well to the final product, but that's the message and the feel that we were going to go for.
&183 Also, Dave Gilbert constantly threatens that he's going to make me animate a dance scene in a game, and it was James that ended up making me animate dancing.
&184 So Dave, you've been beaten to the dancing punch. I'm sorry.

&190 I love this area for a bunch of different reasons. Firstly because it allowed me to draw a lovely seascape vista with nice pink colors that is unlike any other location, any other place in this game.
&191 Secondly, because I was then allowed to blow it to smithereens, which is always fun! And doing a nuclear explosion isn't something I'd ever thought I'd animate in a game, but there we go.

&192 And thirdly because I got to draw a character whose avatar looks like a cross between a Fallout fanboy and a Full Throttle fanboy. Both of those are games which I adore. And to combine them into one weird and silly character was fantastic.
&200 Usually when drawing cityscapes for Technobabylon, I focused on a really blue palette for a really cold electronic feel. Even in areas where it's a little bit greener, I still stuck with it.

&201 But in this location, I didn't feel that the blue tone - the coldness of it - suited an exclusive restaurant where all these top people would come to meet. So I really warmed the color up as you can see in this skyscape.

&210 When James first told me that I was going to be drawing a room full of corposes I had really vivid, bold images of human beings hanging from meathooks and closeups and ribs sticking out and things.
&211 But actually when he showed me the final design, it was really a lot more polite than I was expecting. I'm not disappointed. It probably turned out for the best that we didn't get gratuitous.

&220 A nice thing about doing science fiction or invented, sort of, vehicles and locations, is that even in places where you've got boring areas, like  this simple hallway, you can add a lot of details.
&221 They're only visual noise, but they help break up the flat planes and make a, sort of, more textured thing that make it a lot more interesting.
&230 Ben Chandler (Art & Animation)
&240 One thing I try to avoid if I animate shimmering water on the ceiling or rippling water, as I have done both here, is try to avoid making it look like it's just been pasted onto the scene.
&241 So what I actually do is render both of them outside of photoshop, then paste it into photoshop, and then use adjustment/overlay layers  to make the whole scene feel more cohesive.
&242 It can be quite easy to have water effects stand out badly and look like cheap 90s effects. I'm not sure if I managed to avoided that here, but I've done my utmost!
&1 Greetings! I'm Nathan Allen Pinard and I'm responsible for creating the Music for this game.
&2 I'm also responsible for Sound Design, and some pretty cool vocal effects heard throughout the game.
&3 For the audiophiles out there that are interested in what I use, my main Digital Audio Workstation software is Studio One Pro 2.
&4 I also use several virtual instrument libraries like Hollywood Strings, Omnisphere, CineBrass CORE, Emotional Piano,
&5 Oracle, Project Alpha, Project Bravo, and some others I can't recall at the moment, but quite a few.
&6 I wasn't fully aware of what Trance music should sound like. I can partially understand Latha because she has a great deal of anxiety.
&7 Anxiety in the real world as opposed to trance. Kind of a hard-core form of social anxiety.
&8 I have anxiety myself, so I could relate to it. I sometimes avoid going out as the anxiety gets the best of me.
&9 So I simply asked James if Latha was meant to feel very good while in the Trance.
&10 The answer was yes, so I reflected that blissful feeling with the sort of computery digital feeling in the music. And this is the result.
&11 This ended up being the theme to the entire game as well.
&12 This is the first track I wrote for Technobabylon. I was told that the music in this scene should reflect that "something isn't quite right".
&13 However, it wasn't meant to be obvious what would happen, just that unsettling feeling.
&14 Knowing the character of Latha now though, this entire scene was meant to just show the anxiety she is feeling being in "meatspace".
&15 Using dissonance with muted strings is a useful tactic to show a scene that is tense, but not directly dangerous or exciting. Rather pretty actually.
&16 And I suppose I got that idea from a few iconic composers, such as Jerry Goldsmith, or Bernard Herrmann.
&17 Using wetware in technobabylon is such an important sound design moment, it's used so much, and it's the direct basis of integrating into tech.
&18 In a point-and-click, you generally don't have direct animations for everything. In this case you only see Latha touch something.
&19 This indicates one thing. That she's using wetware with something.
&20 So since there is no animation for that, we use sound design to show what happens.
&21 I literally had a picture of what it looked like. You can almost hear it.
&22 Something organic and gelatinous creeps into the tech you are connecting to, it connects digitally.
&23 And eventually you even hear a UI sound confirming you are connected.
&24 When I got the original VO for Cheffie, it was Jessica Pepper's normal voice. So naturally I had to alter her somehow.
&25 I added a few effects to her, the trance effect, a chorus, and a few other effects.
&26 But what's curious about this voice over, is she actually sang "T.H.E. Foods" in the original audio.
&27 So I imagined in a futuristic world like Technobabylon, that it would be heavily corporate.
&28 So I decided to use her singing as more of a jingle, or some kind of branding, while also including a synth behind her everytime she says it.
&29 I used Melodyne to have her sing the same notes every time, kind of like the NBC thing on TV.
&30 And that just turned out brilliant.
&31 This one was fun. In fact this whole scene was fun. Having to do sound design of a body hitting a car from a building is definitely a challenge.
&32 The scream was a random experiment. I had several friends in the room when inputting that just for fun.
&33 It made them spit their drinks out, so I knew it needed to stay. Having a bit of comedy in an otherwise dark scene, can be pretty useful.
&34 Of course I provided a non-comedy version and a comedy version to James, and naturally...he picked the comedy one.
&35 This entire scene to me, is a bit of a neat placement of various music cues.
&36 There are a number of tracks here that play into each other, that continue as if it's a fully scored timed scene that is static.
&37 You enter the room, the first scene music plays. Then it stops if you wait long enough.
&38 Then to go to the elevator, the body falls, track of suspense plays. That continues and runs out as well if you let it.
&39 Then the scroll up to the office happens, and new music there plays and at this point loops.
&40 If you click through dialogue or rush the scene, the music crossfades anyway, and it's like it was INTENDED.
&41 It ends up working almost like a TV show score. Kinda.
&42 So yes...I'm kinda proud of the music in this scene.
&43 So the subway music is more for a tense, but not directly violent situation. It's very hard to do this in adventure games, as there IS no action.
&44 So really having a "pulse" of something that is happening, along with some peaks in the music works really well for this scene.
&45 You can hear the pulse in the pizzicato, as was as the staccato strings. The peaks are done by the brass at times with slow crescendos.
&46 It fits the dialogue and situation, but doesn't directly say "action is happening". More like...well there is a bomb and you are trying to defuse it.
&47 What a deliciously gruesome scene. This wasn't even this bad at first when I wrote the track. Later on MORE gore was added.
&48 This particular track is important just to show that "oh my god" feeling, and that is what it seems to do.
&49 Also James added to the impact by having the room be dark at first, which was not in the first few builds.
&50 So turning on the light, right on the impact in the music, is even more effective.
&51 This is another scene that had various "pieces" of the music in separate tracks. Each track builds in succession.
&52 This was meant to occur on the growls from the emanation that appears through this scene.
&53 While I probably didn't need to do several tracks, it does give James the ability to move things around if he needs to.
&54 And also for any that decide to click through a  few pieces of dialogue, the music moves with that as well.
&55 This particular music was important, because CEL is a very iconic vision for Technobabylon.
&56 A police/science/tech hybrid that is super clean, with shiny metal surfaces, and lots of...blue.
&57 So this music was kind of meant to reflect that as being a technological marvel.
&58 I don't have much more than that, really I was just trying to write something cool :)
&59 There are three main characters in this game, you have Regis, Lao, and Latha.
&60 However, in some ways I feel Central is the main character of this game.
&61 So engineering the voice for Central was quite important. I didn't just want a standard computer voice.
&62 I wanted something that would reflect that Central's origin is in fact, human.
&63 So we ended up with sort of a human/computer hybrid voice, which is essentially a pitched down vocal to start with.
&64 Mainly because the original voice was kind of adorable. But her acting was very computer like, so pitching her down actually worked well.
&65 You couldn't just say words and it would work, you had to act it out properly with the proper inflections.
&66 And the actress probably doesn't even know her voice has been altered in such a way yet.
&67 So after changing the pitch, autofilter was added, some chorus, and some delay, along with some pitch correction to make it sound artificial.
&68 And there you have it. Central.
&69 This entire section was meant to be pretty. It was meant to be almost like you are in a jungle, or the amazon.
&70 That is exactly what the description James had for me in terms of music.
&71 So I ended up with this New Age style theme, with a bit of sci-fi.
&72 But it's also topped off by some angelic choir, which just seals the deal for this track for me.
&73 This room is loud. It was meant to be.
&74 This sound is this room is borrowed from Gemini Rue from the Weather Tower, which was some sort of print press ambience in real life.
&75 But I added my gas furnace for color!
&76 This is my voice!
&77 It's basically the same effects as Central, but with a male voice.
&78 Obviously I pitched myself down, but the effect is there. And I did it in a more condescending authoritative way.
&79 The very last battle in Gemini Rue involved a percussion based track with very simple background ambience. Using a lot of Taikos.
&80 So this music is actually kind of the same idea, but a little more interesting. It has more of a cyberpunk feel to it.
&81 But on top of that, the main melody is more pleasant, using humming choir, and some synth pads, as well as bells.
&82 While some rather heavy percussion and synth bass is playing in the background.
&83 This adds to the scene a great deal, but doesn't go over the top. Because as I said, there is no real "action" in point-and-clicks.
&84 So instead you just have to make things very tense. And after the music was added to this scene, it definitely does that.
&85 The laser is a small part of this game, but it was really important I make this thing sound interesting.
&86 That sort of "glass cutting sound" along with the musical hum is exactly what I was going for, and it took quite a bit of time to get this.
&87 In fact, it kind of reminds me of the hyperspace jump sound from Homeworld. Which also was quite musical in a way.
&88 So every time someone uses this, it's a bit more pleasant than "Pewwwwwwww!"
&89 All three soldiers in this game are Dave's voice. Each one is pitched slightly so it appears to be a different person.
&90 The hardest part was figuring out the sound of the voice, and what effects would accomplish that sound.
&91 The soliders were meant to be kinda faceless, and have all personality erased. So a bit of ring modulation and other effects took care of that.
&92 The voices are heard, and can be understood, but you can't quite hear the inflections in the voice that give it personality.
&93 Therefore it achieves that sort of "storm trooper" effect. Or a better reference would be the Combine from Half Life 2.
&94 This track is probably one of my favorite tracks I've done, as it takes a very simple chord progression and makes it interesting.
&95 The track has this whole seedy undertone which fit the whole "downtown" appearance in this scene.
&96 The psudeo east coast drum loop added with the pulsing synth bass, going back and forth between two chords in the whole song.
&97 But is also topped off with a very lite synth bell finish.
&98 EDM. Such a hard genre of music to do. Most people don't realize this, and in some cases don't believe it, But EDM and pop is hard.
&99 It's less about the musical writing, and more about sound design. You can come up with a great chord progression and a hook.
&100 But it falls flat if you don't know all the bells and whistles to put in between.
&101 This is essentially the EDM version of the Technobabylon theme. It doesn't sound commercial, but it does have a uniqueness to it.
&102 And I personally like it. That it doesn't sound like commercial dance music.
&103 Oh man. This track. This is the last one I did for Technobabylon. While this track is only about a minute long it took 4 hours to do.
&104 As a comparison, it took like 45 minutes to do the title music in this game.
&105 I postponed it so much because I kept getting ideas. First I thought chip tune music. But then I said no to that, because everyone does chip tune music.
&106 Then I thought, why not get the soundsets for the Sega Genesis? But that turned out to be a bit difficult, and required some fast learning.
&107 Then I remember I did a track a long time ago for a client, known as "Oxhorn" which actually was a bit of a j-pop parody.
&108 It lasted only about 15 seconds, but was hilarious. And that is what James and Dave wanted. So I went into that style for this track.
&109 And this is the result!
&110 The music here isn't exactly music, but it incorporates two sound effect that are known in this type of universe.
&111 At first you hear the geiger counter clicks, and then later the vintage WW2 air raid siren.
&112 Basically, I was going for a Fallout vibe.
&113 The classical piano in the back is performed by Jennifer Thomas.
&114 I always wanted to use Moonlight Sonata in a project, it's probably my favorite classical piece of all time (aside from the Planets of course)
&115 And I felt it really fit here. Because you have a bunch of higher ups, in a glamorous restaurant, eating...human flesh.
&116 Adding this piece of music just makes the whole scene that much more morbid.
&117 Also as a Sound Design note, you'll hear the tone of the track change a bit as you move from room to room.
&118 When I first saw the Aerostat drawings, I understood that this is the future, but not everything changes.
&119 We see this today, with tablets in our hands. Something even more advanced than the padds in Star Trek.
&120 So I feel the Aerostat would fall behind a bit in technology. So I chose the sounds to make the aircraft sound like a turboprop.
&121 The take-off, landing, and idle sounds are various combinations of jet engines and props, as well as a few samples of the Bombardier Q400.
&122 This scene had to be loud and dangerous sounding, as well as dynamic.
&123 So I had two sounds layered here. The overall background ambience of engines, wind, and props.
&124 Combined with the loud engine on the left.
&125 When you stop the engine on the left, you'll notice that goes away, and now you can hear the wind and other engines.
&126 It's not every day that I get to create sound design depicting a man getting chewed to death in a bunch of machinery.
&127 Lots of rattling, bone crunching, and 'glop' sounds make this a bit more graphic than it looks.
&128 The chair room is essentially the life blood of Central. Lots of organic uh...balloons lining the walls. Very creepy looking.
&129 So I wanted to show that in the sound design. You'll notice you can hear sort of digital glitches on the left.
&130 And a bit of...sloppiness on the right.
&131 All backed by a pulsing heartbeat like drone.
&132 The core music here has a very technological sound. In fact, the piece itself is written in 5/4 time.
&133 But the chords I chose don't actually have thirds in them, they are all sus2 chords, which actually kind of gives it a Chrono Trigger vibe.
&134 There are three versions of this track. One in this room, the other within Trance, and a third track which is a more ambient version.
&135 This scene shows a bunch of remnants of all the people that the Mindjacker has killed. I wanted to reflect that in the sound design here.
&136 Most people wouldn't hear it, but the odd sounds you are hearing are actually dialogue from the game.
&137 This scene worked ok with the current core music, but the emotional impact wasn't there.
&138 So I wanted to do a sort of similar feeling that you would hear in a movie.
&139 A simple recurring motif, which in this case is the piano, along with some moving chords, utilizing strings.
&140 I couldn't go too far as it would overcome the dialogue that was happening.
&141 But the idea was to make the player believe that Regis was sacrificing himself, and that was the end of it.
&142 Of course, just afterwards you find out that wasn't the case.

The measure, signed into law by EF Prime Minister Jacqueline Santini at 06:52:80 (15:40pm), is planned to be rolled out over the course of the next four years. Under the scheme, measure of the time of day is to be divided into ten hours, each with 100 minutes, made up of 100 seconds. [

Santini, whose Federalist Party have been one of the keenest supporters of the new policy, greeted the change enthusiastically. 'Computing and commercial time measurement has long been carried out in a metric scale with atomic timing, and the division into 24 hours has itself merely been an arbitrary convention of history.' [

While commonly referred to as 'metric' time, the measurement of a day into periods of ten should more accurately be known as 'decimal' time. Internationally the EF's policy has gained little traction, if not outright criticism, with some leaders condemning the changes as 'unnatural'.

The Oceania Cooperative's government was less emotive, issuing a statement that though the change was 'one demanded by the European voter, which we will respect as a democratic institution', they made clear that the OC has no plans to adopt any similar measures.
